extracted.intended_audience: students and informed readers of political science / American political institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how public opinion operates in American democracy: its salutary effects, necessary supporting conditions, limits and tensions, and the causes/forms of municipal corruption (e.g., party machines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Healthiness of public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The strong point of the American system is the healthiness of public opinion, and the control which it exerts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public opinion's strength keeps down evils that creep into the working of the Constitution and may in time extinguish them; Lincoln's maxim is cited: 'With public sentiment on its side, everything succeeds; with public sentiment against it, nothing succeeds.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity/exposure as a corrective force
rubrics_metrics.description: The genius of universal publicity — a public atmosphere 'fresh, keen, and full of sunlight' — kills many of those noxious germs hatched where politicians congregate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selfishness, injustice, cruelty, tricks and jobs shun the light; to expose them is to defeat them. No serious evils can remain long concealed, and disclosure is half destruction. (Examples and metaphors throughout the chapter.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion as competent authority to determine national ends
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion of a whole nation, a united and tolerably homogeneous nation, is the most competent authority to determine the ends of national policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with European practice where legislatures/cabinets sometimes take decisions the nation later disapproves; in America nothing should commit the nation until it has manifested its wishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous deliberation and discussion beyond elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion secures full discussion of issues and of the characters of men; it listens patiently to all arguments addressed to it and is influenced by eloquence, education, wisdom and experience in the long run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democracy governed through a constantly active public opinion (not solely periodic elections) tends to become patient, tolerant, reasonable and less embittered by class divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions necessary for democratic government to educate citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Along with the mere enjoyment of power there must be found some auspicious conditions: a direct and fairly equal interest in the common welfare; presence of a class respected and competent to guide; absence of religious or race hatreds; a high level of education or at least intelligence; old habits of local self-government; the practice of unlimited free discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without these conditions the educational value of suffrage is small; the habit of voting alone does not suffice to train citizens to use liberty well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational value of public life and active participation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not simply the habit of voting, but the briskness of the whole atmosphere of public life — obtaining information, discussing it, hearing and judging each side — that forms the citizen's intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The polling-booth completes the process, but the daily practice of reading, talking and judging public affairs is what cultivates responsibility and independence of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith in free inquiry and long-run correction
rubrics_metrics.description: A boundless faith in free inquiry and full discussion: admitting temporary errors and delusions but trusting that a nation which has canvassed everything will not ultimately go wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows tolerance of many preliminary experiments and errors because public discussion and inquiry are trusted to correct mistakes over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion as substitute for heavy government
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion's immense power enables Americans 'to get on with but little government' — some evils a law must deal with elsewhere are here averted or cured by the mere force of opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because opinion is not the product of any one class, it discourages class legislation and reduces the necessity for coercive legal measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation of class legislation by national opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: When a particular section clamours for measures to help it, national opinion—recognized by everyone as the arbiter—mitigates these feelings and requires advocates to show their schemes are compatible with the paramount interest of the whole community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents the formation of hostile class-based legislation and fosters the view that justice and equality of opportunity are self-evident principles of national prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention as a weapon against bad or selfish measures
rubrics_metrics.description: If opponents can fix the people's attention on a mischievous bill before it passes, its chances are slight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many corrupt or pernicious schemes hatched in legislatures are abandoned because people will not stand them once attention is focused; examples include President Grant's attempt to annex San Domingo and restraint after the Civil War.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public scrutiny prevents bad appointments when responsibility is clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Where undivided responsibility can be fixed on the appointing authority, public opinion prevents countless bad appointments for which politicians intrigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In places where public opinion is active (e.g., the North), leading posts are seldom filled by bad men; where opinion is absent or indifferent (e.g., the South post-war), corrupt patronage flourishes. Comparison made with British regional differences as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion as a reserve force in foreign policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion watches the language and acts of the State Department and will support vindicating Americans' rights but check any demand or act going beyond legal rights that might embroil the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a caution against rash or overreaching foreign policies; ordinary citizens are ready to check diplomatically imprudent actions even while opposing foreign interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assimilation of immigrants through opinion and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Republic dissolves and assimilates foreign bodies quickly; the all-pervading force of opinion, public schools and newspapers transmute newcomers into Americans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Younger immigrants who learn English and are dispersed among natives become indistinguishable from natives; public schooling and the press are key instruments of assimilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion fosters moderation, patience and respect for opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens are disposed to try soft means first, to expect others to bow to the force of opinion; opposition does not incense them and danger does not hurry them into precipitate courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beaten minorities often take defeat well; the public grows more temperate, mellow, tolerant, and 'respects itself too much to wish to silence any voice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between popular voice and great leadership (hero-worship)
rubrics_metrics.description: The all-subduing power of the popular voice may dwarf aspiring individualities but the American people also hunger for and exalt great men, sometimes following showy geniuses despite intellectual or moral shortcomings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public opinion can both suppress visionary leadership and simultaneously produce intense loyalty or hero-worship (examples: Clay, Jefferson, Webster, Lincoln, Jackson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes and mechanics of municipal perversion (machine politics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid immigration of poor and ignorant foreigners who receive votes, are cohesive and led by their own leaders, combined with neglect of local politics by wealthier classes, transfers power to rougher elements and enables laborious organization that fosters party machines and corruption (e.g., Tammany in New York).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Growth and composition of urban populations, the organization of newcomers, and the diversion of elites' attention from municipal affairs are identified as key causal factors; municipal corruption differs from European cities in character and scale.
